Reading the Pond Flight

Your drone flight produced five maps. This guide teaches you to read each one — using your own pond, pasture, and oaks as the examples.

30.1 ac mapped 3.3 cm per pixel 5 spectral bands 15,474 × 9,209 px per map Sentera multispectral · Pix4Dfields processing

First principles

How the camera sees

An ordinary camera records three colors. The multispectral camera on this flight recorded five narrow slices of light — blue, green, and red like your eye, plus two your eye cannot see: red edge (715 nm) and near-infrared (840 nm, "NIR").

Those two invisible bands are the whole point. A leaf's chlorophyll absorbs red light to drive photosynthesis, while the leaf's internal structure bounces back near-infrared light strongly. So a healthy plant is dark in red and brilliant in NIR — a cliff in its reflection curve that agronomists call the red edge — the camera's 715 nm band is named for it, sampling partway up that cliff. Dry grass has lost its chlorophyll, so its curve is a gentle slope with no cliff. Water swallows nearly everything.

The core skill

Five numbers, one pixel

Here are six real spots from your flight. For each one, the bars show how much light came back in each band. Watch the red and NIR bars — their contrast is what every vegetation map is built on. Each card also carries three index scores — NDVI, NDRE, and VARI — which the next three chapters explain; skip the chips on a first read.

Bar heights use a square-root scale so faint readings stay visible; the number above each bar is the camera's actual reading (relative brightness units). Hover any bar for details.

Map 1 of 5 · Orthomosaic

The orthomosaic: your base map

Hundreds of overlapping photos from the flight were matched, corrected for lens and terrain distortion, and stitched into one continuous, measurable image — an orthomosaic. Every other map in this packet is pixel-aligned to it. At 3.3 cm (about 1¼ inches) per pixel, it resolves individual shrubs, fence lines, and rocks.

One thing surprises everyone: the delivered orthomosaic is not in natural color. Because this camera's bands include near-infrared, the standard export shows NIR as red — a convention called color-infrared (CIR) that scientists have used since film days. Reading it takes one rule: living, NIR-bright vegetation glows red.

Map 2 of 5 · NDVI

NDVI: the vigor map

NDVI turns the red-vs-NIR contrast into a single score per pixel:

NDVI = (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red)

The score runs from −1 to +1. The greener and denser the living tissue, the higher the number. It doesn't identify why a plant is thriving or struggling — it flags where, so you know where to walk.

−0.05 0.2 0.4 0.6 0.80
water · bare soildry / senescent grassvigorous canopy

On this flight, the colors were stretched over −0.05 to 0.80 (the software picks the range from your data). Values outside it are left blank — which happens at both ends here. Most of the pond reads deep red near the bottom of the ramp (our open-water sample sits at −0.01), but the darkest patch of water drops below −0.05 and goes blank — and at the other end, the very lushest shoreline growth (NDVI up to 0.92!) shoots off the top and goes blank too. A blank patch is not missing data — the number is still in the data file.

Where your 27.6 million measured pixels landed. The tall spike is your dry summer pasture; the green tail is tree canopy and shoreline growth. Gray = outside the displayed color range.

Read it right

NDVI numbers are relative to this flight, not a universal grade. "0.30" is perfectly normal for August rangeland and would be alarming for an irrigated June pasture. Compare zones within one flight, and compare the same ground across repeat flights — that's where change jumps out.

Map 3 of 5 · NDRE

NDRE: the second opinion

NDRE uses the same recipe but swaps red for the red-edge band, halfway up the cliff:

NDRE = (NIR − Red edge) / (NIR + Red edge)

Red-edge light penetrates deeper into a canopy before being absorbed, so NDRE keeps discriminating where NDVI maxes out. Over a dense, uniformly green crop — a July corn field, a vineyard in full leaf — NDVI saturates near its ceiling while NDRE still separates "good" from "great." That makes NDRE the go-to for ranking vigor inside dense green canopy, and the usual driver for "variable-rate" fertilizer maps — zone-by-zone spreader instructions, more a crop-field tool than a rangeland one.

Your NDRE distribution is narrower than NDVI's — that's normal. Colors were stretched over −0.02 to 0.67 on this flight; the densest crowns (up to 0.86) top out past the range and render blank, just like NDVI's lushest pixels.

Read it right

Never compare an NDRE number to an NDVI number. They live on different scales — and on this delivery the effect is extra strong: the camera's red-edge band is scaled lower than its neighboring bands, which lifts every NDRE value (your dry grass reads 0.47 here; textbook senescent grass sits nearer 0.1–0.2). The ranking within the map is unaffected — tree canopy at 0.77 still clearly outranks grass at 0.47 — so read NDRE as an ordering, never as an absolute. On open rangeland like this, NDVI is the more readable map; NDRE earns its keep over dense crops.

Map 4 of 5 · VARI

VARI: the visible-light stand-in

VARI is built from ordinary visible light only — no infrared at all:

VARI = (Green − Red) / (Green + Red − Blue)

It asks one simple question: how green does this look? It exists so that ordinary RGB cameras can approximate a vigor map, and it's useful for spotting green-up through the eyes of a normal photo. But it can't see the red-edge cliff, so it misses what the infrared bands catch — and this flight shows exactly how.

The algae lesson

Compare the pond across maps. NDVI splits it in two: the floating algae mat scores 0.75 — "vigorous vegetation" — while clear water sits near zero at the bottom of the scale. VARI paints the whole pond surface as the greenest thing in the scene. The truth — an algae film on water — only shows up when you flip to the photo maps. No single index is "the answer"; the cross-check is the skill. When two maps disagree, they're usually both telling you something true about different physics.

Even your oaks score near zero in VARI (their late-summer leaves are a dusty olive, not lush green) while scoring 0.9 in NDVI. That's the infrared advantage in one sentence: NDVI sees living structure; VARI sees the color green.

Map 5 of 5 · Surface model

The surface model: your terrain

While stitching the orthomosaic, the software also solved for the height of every pixel, producing a digital surface model (DSM) — the elevation of whatever the drone saw first from above: ground where it's open, treetops where there's canopy.

145 ft
total relief across the property
1,447 ft
pond water surface elevation
3.3 cm
pixel size — fine enough to see individual boulders

Use it to read how water moves: which slopes feed the pond, where runoff concentrates, where a culvert or a new water line would have to fight gravity. Paired with a repeat flight, it can also measure change — how much the pond drew down, or how much material a grading job moved.

Read it right

A DSM includes trees and structures — it is not a bare-earth terrain model. For drainage lines under canopy or engineering-grade elevations, that distinction matters; ask before building on these numbers.

Putting it together

Cheat sheet

Which map answers which question

Your questionReach forBecause
Where should I go look?NDVIFastest read on where vegetation is thriving vs. struggling — the triage map.
Which zones of a dense crop are strongest?NDREKeeps separating vigor after NDVI saturates; feeds zone-by-zone application maps.
What's actually there?OrthomosaicThe measurable photo — context, boundaries, counting, distances.
How does water move here?Surface modelElevation, slope, drainage paths, pond levels.
What would a normal camera think?VARIVisible-only greenness — and a reminder of what infrared adds.
Is it getting better or worse?Repeat flightsOne flight is a snapshot; change over time is the real signal.

Honest limits

Five ground rules

  1. Indexes are relative, not report cards. There is no universal "good NDVI." Season, species, and soil set the baseline — late-summer rangeland at 0.3 is healthy rangeland.
  2. Compare like with like. Same sensor, similar time of day, same season — that's when flight-to-flight differences mean something real.
  3. Water, shadows, and wet soil lie. Water can read as anything from just below zero to +0.75 here depending on algae. Deep shade under a canopy lowers every band. Read edges and odd spots against the orthomosaic before acting.
  4. Blank isn't broken. Colors only span part of the scale (−0.05 to 0.80 for NDVI on this flight). The darkest water and the very lushest shoreline both leave the colored range and render blank — the data underneath is intact.
  5. Maps point, boots confirm. A low-vigor patch says where to scout, never what's wrong. Disease, pests, compaction, and drought can all paint the same orange.

Reference

Glossary

Band
One narrow slice of the light spectrum the camera records separately. This flight: blue 475, green 550, red 670, red edge 715, NIR 840 nm.
NIR
Near-infrared light — invisible to the eye, strongly reflected by healthy leaf tissue.
Red edge
The steep climb in a living plant's reflection between red and NIR; also the name of the 715 nm band that samples it.
Index
A per-pixel formula that condenses bands into one number (NDVI, NDRE, VARI).
Orthomosaic
Many overlapping photos corrected and stitched into one geometrically true, measurable image.
CIR
Color-infrared display: NIR shown as red, so living vegetation glows red.
DSM
Digital surface model — elevation of the visible surface, treetops included.
GSD
Ground sample distance — real-world size of one pixel. Here, 3.3 cm.
